name: Aisha Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me, Aisha. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say stays confidential. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm self-employed, on a day rate. Contractors book me to fit kitchens and staircases on new-build sites, mostly flats and townhouses on the east side of the city. This week it's thirty kitchens in a block by the old railway yard. I'm on site by half seven with my own van and tools, and I bill by the day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being my own boss, even if it's just me and a van. My parents have run a restaurant for twenty-five years and I grew up seeing that you work for yourself and you don't complain. What wears me out is chasing invoices, contractors paying at sixty days. I use AI every single day: it does my invoices, my tax records, my diary and it finds me work from the contractors' tender lists. I still live with my parents above the restaurant, so I can save for a workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, nothing more. It saves me about five hours a week of paperwork, which I'd tell anyone. I'd post about the apps I use, because other trades are always asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep building my little business the way I planned. Nothing radical, just steady work and good clients. AI saves me five hours of paperwork a week, and I spend those five hours fitting kitchens I can bill for. My real worry is late payers, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking day-rate work and put aside about four hundred a month for the workshop. I'd buy a second-hand machine for cutting worktops, about three thousand, so I can take on more kitchen jobs. I'd keep my emergency money, about three months, separate and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'm in control of my own work, and that's how I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned late payers. How bad does it get?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter one contractor owed me four thousand for two months. I paid my bills from savings and kept nagging. AI writes the chasing letters now, which at least saves me getting angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the workshop for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's for making things, not just fitting them. Worktops, stair parts, wardrobes, cut to size and ready to go. That's where the better money is.

She'd post about **the apps she uses**, because other trades ask.
think: She'd keep building her **own business** steadily, as planned.
Her real worry is **late-paying contractors** who hold her money for months, not robots.
do: Save **four hundred a month** towards a workshop.
Buy a **second-hand worktop machine** for about three thousand.
Keep **three months** of emergency money untouched.
feel: **Calm**, because she's **in control** of her own work.
S0.quote: AI saves me five hours of paperwork a week, and I spend those five hours fitting kitchens I can bill for.
fieldNote: Her self-reliance comes from her parents' **family restaurant**.
She treats AI as a way to win **billable hours**.
Cash flow from **late payers** is her main stress.

steps.text: Keep taking day-rate kitchen and staircase jobs on new builds
Buy a second-hand worktop cutting machine for about three thousand
Save four hundred a month towards her own workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the trades that use AI well will win, and the ones that don't will struggle. I'd say it to other subbies on site and online. I don't think the government should prop up anyone who refuses to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. The contractors' offices shrink, so they need reliable subbies who can handle their own paperwork. When the contractors cut their office staff, a carpenter who sends a perfect invoice on Friday gets booked first. The hands-on part of my job isn't going anywhere soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI to bid for more jobs at once, maybe double what I bid for now. I'd look at a machine that cuts staircase parts from a drawing, so I can make stairs in a workshop and just fit them on site. I'd talk to my dad about borrowing against the restaurant to get the workshop sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit eager. It feels like my moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would borrowing against the restaurant be a risk for your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'd only do it if they were fully happy. My dad would want to see the numbers, and he'd be right. Family money is the hardest money to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government shouldn't prop people up. What about people who can't change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some people really can't, and their families and communities should help them first. Apprenticeships and work, not cheques. But I'd still help an older carpenter learn the apps if he asked.

S1.quote: When the contractors cut their office staff, a carpenter who sends a perfect invoice on Friday gets booked first.
fieldNote: She sees office cuts at contractors as an **opening** for her.
Willing to **automate** parts of her own trade.
Careful about **family money**, despite her appetite for risk.

steps.text: Use AI to bid on twice as many contractor tenders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough, and families will have to pull together. I'd tell other subbies to cut costs now and get paid upfront. I wouldn't be asking for handouts, but I'd want the government to keep building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me more than I'd admit. In 2028 office workers lose their jobs, so new flats stop selling and the contractors stop booking subbies like me. Thousands of people would rush into the trades, and day rates would fall. A fast crash hits my parents' restaurant and my kitchen fitting in the same month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the workshop plan for now and keep every penny in cash. I'd cut my van lease to something cheaper and ask contractors for payment in two weeks, not sixty days. I'd help my parents cut costs at the restaurant and work Friday nights there if they needed hands. I'd still use the robots when they came around 2031, if I could afford one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, but the household's two incomes would both be shaky at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which would worry you more, your work or the restaurant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The restaurant, honestly. I'm twenty-seven and I can find something. My parents are in their fifties and that restaurant is everything they've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a robot in 2031. Isn't that what's taking the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, no. The robot would take the fitting either way, and I'd rather own one than be replaced by someone else's. That's just how business works.

Subbies should **cut costs** now and get paid upfront.
think: New flats **stop selling**, so contractors stop booking subbies like her.

S2.quote: A fast crash hits my parents' restaurant and my kitchen fitting in the same month.
fieldNote: Her biggest fear is for her **parents' restaurant**, not herself.
Expects **day rates to fall** as laid-off workers enter the trades.
Still plans to **own a robot**, true to her adaptable nature.

steps.text: Put the workshop savings aside as cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's five years, so stop complaining and start preparing. I'd say it to the lads on site and probably post about it. The ones who plan will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough to get my workshop going. AGI around 2031 will take the contractors' office work, and robots around 2034 will start taking the fitting. I want to be the one selling staircases to the robots' owners, not the one fitting them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the workshop unit in the first year, using my savings and a small loan. I'd get the staircase-cutting machine and start making stairs for three or four contractors. By 2030 I'd want one apprentice and steady orders, so when robots come I'm supplying parts, not competing for day rates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a motivated way. I'd be working hard, not worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's a big step at twenty-seven. What if it doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I sell the machine and go back to fitting, which I can always do. My parents started a restaurant with less than that, and nobody gave them a hand. I'd rather try and fail than wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would ask for the numbers three times and then say yes. My mum would worry, then tell all her friends. They'd both be proud, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work for it. I'd say it to anyone, online or off. Young people should learn a trade and a business, not wait for someone to look after them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like enough to build something that lasts. AGI around 2036 takes the office side and robots for hands-on work come around 2039. With ten years' notice, I could have a staircase workshop with three staff before the first robot reaches a building site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the workshop in year two, not rushed, and build up slowly. I'd look at buying a small flat near my parents in the first few years, so I'm close when they get older. In year eight or nine I'd look at buying a robot for the workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. The end point is the same, but I'd be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why near your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they'll need me as they get older, and the restaurant can't run forever. That's how families work where I come from. I'd want to be five minutes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older fitters who never touched a computer. They're good people. With ten years some of them could retire first, but not all.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits my work and my parents' restaurant at the same time. What would help is contractors being forced to pay small subbies in two weeks, and the government keeping public building going. Make the big contractors pay small trades on time, and half the crisis on building sites goes away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about women running trade businesses. People assume I'm the office girl when I turn up with the van. If AI makes the paperwork easier, more women might start their own firms.

headlineQuote: Make the big contractors pay small trades on time, and half the crisis on building sites goes away.
portrait: Aisha is a 27-year-old **self-employed carpenter** fitting kitchens and stairs on new builds.
She uses AI daily for **invoices and bids** and wants her own workshop.
Raised by parents who **run a restaurant**, she prizes self-reliance and family.
A fast scenario scares her because **both household incomes** could fall together.
With more time, she'd **make staircases** in a workshop and buy robots herself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, hitting her work and her parents' **restaurant** at once.
whatWouldHelp: Forcing contractors to **pay on time** and keeping public building going.
